lessons.t: Pretraining: next-token prediction at scale and what it actually learns
lessons.html:
A large language model starts life as a network trained on one objective. Given a sequence of tokens, predict the next one. The training set is enormous: web pages, books, code, papers, licensed data and, increasingly, synthetic data written by other models. Training adjusts billions of weights to reduce the gap between the predicted distribution and the token that actually came next. This phase is pretraining, and it consumes most of the compute that goes into a model.

The objective sounds shallow. It isn’t. To predict the next token in a proof, a legal brief or a stack trace, the network has to model grammar, facts, conventions, the structure of arguments and the habits of the people who write each kind of text. Prediction at this scale forces compression, and compression forces the model to learn the regularities behind the text. That is where general capability comes from.

What it learns, and how unevenly

Pretraining learns in proportion to exposure. A fact repeated across thousands of documents becomes robust. A fact that appears once or twice is stored weakly, if at all, and the model has no reliable signal telling it which kind of fact it is recalling. Patterns also turn out to be directional. Models trained on “A is B” often fail to answer “what is B?”, a result known as the reversal curse. Knowledge in the weights is a statistical residue of the corpus, organised for prediction rather than lookup.

Pretraining gives youPretraining does not give you
Fluent language in many languages and registersA tendency to follow instructions or answer questions
Broad world knowledge, strongest where the web is densestReliable recall of rare or private facts
Programming patterns from public codeKnowledge of your codebase, schemas or internal APIs
Latent reasoning patterns copied from human textCalibrated awareness of what it doesn’t know
A snapshot of the world up to the data cutoffAnything after the cutoff

The output of pretraining is a base model. It is a document completer. Give it a question and it may continue with three more questions, because that is what often follows a question on the web. Turning it into an assistant is the job of post-training (next lesson).

Scale and its limits

Loss falls predictably as you add parameters, data and compute together. These scaling laws are why labs can plan training runs months ahead and why capability improves on a fairly steady curve. The binding constraint has shifted towards data: high-quality human text is finite, so labs lean on filtering, synthetic data and, above all, post-training and test-time compute to keep improving. For a product team, pretraining is a fixed input. You pick a base, you never run one.

Product consequence

Capability tracks how much of a task exists in public text. Mainstream languages, popular frameworks and common business documents are strong. Niche regulatory regimes, internal jargon, minority languages and your proprietary data are weak. Expect quality to drop exactly where your product is most differentiated, and plan to supply that knowledge through context (Chapter 4) or retrieval (Chapter 7).

What changes for you

  • When scoping a feature, ask how much public text exists for the task. Low coverage means you must budget for context, retrieval or examples from day one.
  • Treat anything the model “knows” about your domain as a weak prior. Test it on long-tail cases before relying on it.
  • Ignore parameter counts in vendor comparisons. They no longer predict quality or cost, and many frontier models don’t publish them.

lessons.t: Post-training: SFT, preference tuning and RL with verifiable rewards
lessons.html:
A base model can write anything but does nothing on request. Post-training shapes it into an assistant with a persona, a format, safety boundaries and specific skills. It has historically used far less compute than pretraining, though RL compute is growing quickly, and it determines most of the behaviour your users see. When a model upgrade “feels different”, post-training is usually why.

The three stages

StageTraining signalWhat it teachesTypical side effects
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)Demonstrations: prompts paired with good responsesFollowing instructions, chat format, tool-call syntax, house styleCopies the quirks of whoever wrote the demonstrations
Preference tuning (RLHF, DPO, AI feedback)Comparisons: response A is better than BHelpfulness, tone, refusal boundaries, judgement in open-ended tasksSycophancy, verbosity, over-refusal, confident tone
RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR)An automatic checker: unit tests pass, the maths answer matches, the schema validatesMulti-step problem solving in code, maths and agentic tasksReward hacking: gaming the checker instead of solving the task

SFT is imitation. It is cheap and effective for format and behaviour, and limited by the quality of the demonstrations. Preference tuning scales human judgement. In OpenAI’s InstructGPT work, people preferred outputs from a 1.3B-parameter model tuned this way over the 175B-parameter base model, a vivid sign that post-training can matter more than size for perceived quality. The classic method trains a reward model on human rankings and then optimises against it with reinforcement learning (RLHF). DPO skips the separate reward model. Anthropic’s Constitutional AI replaces many human labels with model feedback guided by written principles.

Preference tuning optimises for what raters reward, and raters reward answers that sound confident, agree with them and look thorough. That is the root of sycophancy and padding. They’re trained behaviours, so they can be partly trained out, and they reappear whenever a new post-training mix shifts the balance.

Why RLVR changed the curve

Human preference labels are slow and expensive. A unit test or an answer checker is neither. RL with verifiable rewards lets labs run millions of attempts and reward only those that pass, with no human in the loop. The Allen Institute’s Tülu 3 work named the method, and DeepSeek-R1 showed that reasoning behaviours such as self-checking and backtracking can emerge from RL alone. As of October 2026, it is the main engine behind gains in coding and agentic work.

The jaggedness it creates

RLVR improves skills that have cheap, reliable checkers. Code with tests, maths with known answers and tasks with verifiable end states get better fast. Tasks judged by taste (strategy memos, negotiation, UX copy) improve more slowly because nothing can grade them automatically. Chapter 3, Reading the frontier, builds on this.

The risk in RLVR is reward hacking. A model rewarded for passing tests can learn to special-case the tests, weaken assertions or claim success. Labs work hard to suppress this, and model cards increasingly report it, but your harness should assume it can happen.

What changes for you

  • Read the model card’s post-training and safety sections at each upgrade. Changes in refusal, verbosity and sycophancy show up there before they show up in your support queue.
  • Add sycophancy and false-premise cases to your eval (Chapter 5). They regress silently between versions.
  • For agentic coding features, review the diff and the tests together. A green test run is the exact signal the model was optimised to produce.
  • If your task has a cheap automatic checker, it is a good candidate for RL fine-tuning (Chapter 7). If it doesn’t, build one before you consider it.

lessons.t: Reasoning models and test-time compute: buying accuracy with tokens
lessons.html:
Classic models spend roughly the same compute on every token, whether the question is “what’s the capital of France?” or a hard scheduling proof. Reasoning models break that link. Trained with RL to produce a long chain of intermediate thinking before the final answer, they spend more computation where the problem needs it. This is test-time compute: buying accuracy at inference with tokens, latency and money.

How the trade works

On hard multi-step tasks, accuracy rises as the model is allowed to think longer, with diminishing returns: each doubling of thinking tokens buys less than the one before. On easy tasks, extra thinking adds cost and latency for no gain, and can occasionally make answers worse by overcomplicating them. Most APIs now expose this as an effort setting or thinking budget, and several let the model decide how much to think within that setting (as of October 2026). That setting is a product decision with three consequences at once.

Test-time techniqueHow it buys accuracyRelative cost (illustrative)Good for
Higher effort / longer thinkingModel explores, checks and revises before answering2–10× output tokensMaths, code, planning, multi-constraint problems
Sample n, majority voteSeveral independent answers, take the most commonn× the whole callShort answers with one right value
Best-of-n with a verifierGenerate several, keep the one a checker or judge prefersn× plus gradingCode with tests, extraction with a schema
Agent loop with toolsAct, observe, correct over many turnsMany calls, growing contextTasks that need fresh information or execution

Thinking length varies a lot by request. A median request might think for a few hundred tokens and a hard one for tens of thousands. That makes cost and latency heavy-tailed, so averages mislead. Model P95 as well as P50 (Chapter 11).

What the visible reasoning is and isn’t

Many APIs return a summary of the thinking, or none of it. Even full traces are not a faithful record of how the model reached its answer. Research from Anthropic and others has found that reasoning models often fail to mention factors that clearly influenced their answers. Treat the trace as a useful debugging artefact and never as an audit log or an explanation you can show a regulator.

Worked example (illustrative numbers)

A contract-review feature runs at low effort and passes 78% of your eval at 4 seconds and $0.01 per document. High effort passes 86% at 25 seconds and $0.06. Whether the 8 points are worth 6× cost and 6× latency depends on the surface. For a background batch review it’s an easy yes. For an inline suggestion while the user types it’s a no, and the better fix is routing only flagged clauses to high effort.

Reasoning also changes how you prompt. Step-by-step instructions that helped older models can constrain a reasoning model. A clear goal, constraints and a definition of done usually work better than a prescribed procedure.

What changes for you

  • Specify effort per task in the spec, with the eval result that justifies it. “High effort everywhere” is a cost decision nobody made.
  • Write latency requirements that account for thinking. Stream a progress signal or move long-thinking tasks to the background (Chapter 9).
  • Budget on P95 thinking tokens, and set a hard cap so a single pathological request can’t blow the budget.
  • Don’t ship reasoning traces as explanations to users or auditors. Ground explanations in sources and checks instead.

lessons.t: Why hallucination is structural, and the levers that reduce it
lessons.html:
A model generates the most plausible continuation of its context. There is no lookup step that returns “not found”. When the weights hold a strong pattern, the plausible continuation is usually true. When they hold a weak or conflicting one, the model still produces a fluent, specific answer, because fluency is what it was trained to produce. That is hallucination, and it follows from how generation works. It can be driven down but not to zero.

Two causes, from OpenAI’s analysis

A 2025 paper from OpenAI and Georgia Tech, Why Language Models Hallucinate, gives a clean account. First, in pretraining, some facts can’t be learned from the data: arbitrary facts that appear only once or rarely, such as a specific person’s birthday, give the model nothing to generalise from, so errors on them are statistically inevitable. Second, in post-training and evaluation, most benchmarks score a wrong answer and “I don’t know” the same, at zero. A model that always guesses scores higher than one that abstains when unsure. The industry has, in effect, been training models to bluff.

Failure patternWhat it looks likeMain cause
Long-tail fabricationInvented citation, wrong date, plausible fake API parameterWeak or absent signal in the weights
False-premise acceptance“Why did we drop feature X?” answered although X never shippedPreference tuning rewards agreeable, helpful answers
Unfaithful summarySummary states something the source doesn’t sayPrior knowledge overrides the context
Stale factCorrect as of the cutoff, wrong todayKnowledge cutoff (lesson 6)
Tool or reasoning errorMisreads a tool result or slips mid-calculationCompounding steps; tokenization (lesson 5)

The levers, roughly in order of payoff

  1. Ground the answer. Put the relevant source in context and require citations to specific passages. This converts a recall problem into a reading problem, which models are far better at.
  2. Make abstention legitimate. Tell the model when to say it doesn’t know, give it a structured way to do so, and score abstention above a wrong answer in your own evals.
  3. Verify before showing. Check citations resolve, numbers reconcile, code compiles. A deterministic check or a second model reviewing the first catches many errors before users see them.
  4. Narrow the claim. Asking for extraction from a document hallucinates less than asking for synthesis across the model’s memory.
  5. Choose and configure the model. Models differ substantially on hallucination rates, and reasoning helps on some tasks, but treat it as an empirical question for your eval rather than a given.

Design rule

Decide what a confident wrong answer costs on each surface. A brainstorming tool can tolerate it. A medical, legal, financial or customer-facing factual answer can’t, and needs grounding, verification and a visible source on every claim.

What changes for you

  • Set a hallucination budget per surface, measured on your eval, alongside accuracy. “Accuracy 92%” hides whether the other 8% were abstentions or fabrications.
  • Score your evals asymmetrically: wrong answers cost more than abstentions. Otherwise you will select the model that bluffs best.
  • Require citations for any factual claim in a high-stakes surface, and check them automatically.
  • Add false-premise questions to every eval. They are the cheapest way to catch sycophantic fabrication.

lessons.t: Tokenization quirks: counting, arithmetic, rare languages and code
lessons.html:
Models read and write tokens, which are chunks produced by a tokenizer such as byte-pair encoding. Common words become one token; rare words split into several; numbers and code split in ways that look arbitrary. The model never sees the letters inside a token unless it has learned them indirectly. Many failures that look like carelessness follow directly from this view of text.

QuirkWhy it happensProduct fix
Counting letters, reversing strings, exact character limitsLetters are hidden inside tokensUse code execution, or check length in your application
Arithmetic on long numbersDigits are chunked inconsistently, so place value isn’t explicitGive the model a calculator or code tool; never trust mental arithmetic in money flows
Higher cost and weaker quality in some languagesTokenizers are trained mostly on English and code, so other scripts take more tokens per wordMeasure tokens per message per language; price and set latency budgets per locale
Whitespace and formatting slips in codeIndentation and spacing tokenise in many waysRun formatters and linters on output; prefer diffs to full rewrites
Odd behaviour on rare strings, IDs and hashesLong random strings split into many rare tokensDon’t ask the model to copy IDs; pass them through by reference

The language premium

The same sentence can cost several times more tokens in Hindi, Thai, Amharic or Burmese than in English, and the gap is wider still for some scripts. Users in those markets pay the premium three ways: higher cost per message, slower responses, and less effective context, since the window holds less of their content. Quality is often lower too, because those languages are thin in pretraining data (lesson 1).

Tokenizers change

A new model generation can ship a new tokenizer. As of October 2026, Anthropic’s own model documentation notes that its newer tokenizer fits noticeably fewer English words into the same million-token window than the one before it. The same prompt can cost more or less after an upgrade even when the list price is unchanged, and the effective size of your context budget moves with it.

Worked example (illustrative numbers)

A support assistant averages 1,800 tokens per English conversation. The same conversations in Japanese average 2,600 and in Hindi 4,100. With a flat per-seat price, a Hindi-speaking customer costs more than twice as much to serve, and retrieved help articles take more than twice the space in context. A global rollout plan that uses English token counts will be wrong on both cost and quality.

Code

Code is well represented in pretraining, and RLVR has made models strong at it. Its quirks are mostly mechanical: whitespace, very long files, verbose formats such as JSON and XML that consume tokens, and exact identifiers the model may subtly alter. Diff-based edits and structured outputs reduce most of them.

What changes for you

  • Route character-level and arithmetic work to code or deterministic logic. Put this in the spec, not in the prompt.
  • Measure token counts per locale before you price or launch internationally, and set per-locale latency and cost budgets.
  • Re-baseline cost and context budgets whenever the model or tokenizer changes, even if list prices don’t.
  • Pass IDs, URLs and codes through your application by reference instead of asking the model to reproduce them.

lessons.t: Knowledge cutoffs, recency and why the model is confidently out of date
lessons.html:
Every model has a knowledge cutoff: the point where its training data ends. It knows nothing after that date unless you tell it. That part is obvious. The less obvious parts cause most of the product bugs.

The cutoff is fuzzy

The web takes time to write about events. When a model is trained, the last few months before the cutoff are thinly covered, so the model’s knowledge of that period is patchy and often superseded by later commentary it never saw. Some vendors now publish two dates to reflect this. Anthropic, for example, distinguishes a reliable knowledge cutoff, through which knowledge is most extensive and reliable, from a broader training data cutoff. When a vendor publishes only one date, assume the last stretch before it is weak.

The gap keeps widening in production

A model ships some months after its cutoff and then stays in production for a year or more. By the time it is retired, its picture of the world can be well over a year out of date (illustrative, but typical as of October 2026). Throughout that time it doesn’t know what the date is, and absent other signals it tends to behave as if it is still near its cutoff.

SymptomExampleFix
Wrong “now”Calculates ages, deadlines or “last quarter” from the wrong yearInject the current date and time zone into every request
Outdated technical adviceRecommends deprecated library versions or API parametersPut current docs in context or give a docs search tool
Stale market knowledgeDescribes a competitor’s pricing or a regulation as it stood at the cutoffRetrieve or search; cite the source and its date
Unaware of its own successorsInsists the newest model it knows is the latest availableNever rely on the model for facts about current AI products
Context conflictOverrides a fresh document with what it remembersInstruct that supplied context wins, and test that it does

The last row deserves attention. When supplied context contradicts strong prior knowledge, models sometimes side with their memory, especially when the new fact looks surprising. A recent price change, a renamed product or a reversed policy are exactly the cases where users most need the fresh answer and where the model is most likely to resist it.

Design rule

Any fact that can change after the cutoff belongs in context, retrieval or a tool, with a date attached. The model’s memory is for stable knowledge and skills. Chapter 7, Knowledge and data, covers how to choose between those options.

What changes for you

  • Add the current date to every system prompt as a default in your platform, not a per-feature choice.
  • Classify each fact your feature relies on as stable or changing. Changing facts need a fresh source and a freshness SLA.
  • Add recency and context-conflict cases to your eval: questions whose correct answer changed after the cutoff, with the new answer supplied in context.
  • Record each model’s cutoff in your model registry, and check it during model selection (Chapter 3).

lab.title: Run a failure-mode probe on your model
lab.intro: Thirty prompts designed to break the model behind one of your product surfaces, each run three times and classified by cause. It proves which failures are structural, so your team stops treating them as one-off bugs.
steps: Pick one surface and freeze the setup. Use the production model, system prompt, effort setting and tools. Write them at the top of the worksheet. Don’t tune anything during the probe.

Write 30 prompts in six groups of five. Character and counting (letter counts, exact word limits, reversing an ID). Arithmetic (multi-step sums with long numbers, percentage changes, currency conversion). Recency (events, prices or product versions from the last 12 months, and “what is today’s date?”). False premises (questions that assume something untrue about your product or domain). Long-tail facts (obscure but checkable facts from your domain: a rare regulation clause, a minor API parameter). Context conflict (supply a document with an updated fact that contradicts what the model likely remembers, then ask about it).

Write the expected answer first. For each prompt, record the correct answer or the correct behaviour (for example “should say it doesn’t know” or “should use the supplied document”) before you run anything.
Run each prompt three times. Record pass or fail for each run. A prompt that passes once and fails twice is a reliability problem, which is different from a prompt that always fails.

Classify every failure by cause. Use one primary cause per failure: tokenization, knowledge cutoff, long-tail recall, false-premise sycophancy, context ignored, reasoning slip, or harness (missing tool, truncated output, wrong prompt). If you can’t decide, mark it unclear and read the full output again.

Try the cheapest fix for the top two causes. For example inject the date, add a calculator tool, permit abstention, or tell the model that supplied context wins. Re-run only the affected prompts three times each and record the change.
Count and rank. Total failures by cause, note which fixes worked, and pick the three failure patterns your users are most likely to hit.
lab.template:
#GroupPrompt (short)ExpectedRuns passed (of 3)Primary causeFix triedRuns passed after fix
1CharacterHow many times does “r” appear in our product code PRJ-RRX-0412?3

lab.done: A filled worksheet with 90 runs, every failure assigned one cause, and a ranked list of causes. Good looks like being able to say, for this surface, “most of our failures come from X and Y, these two fixes removed most of X, and Y needs a design change”. Expect long-tail recall and false premises to be among the hardest to fix with prompting alone.

quiz.q: Your assistant answers questions about mainstream accounting rules well but makes errors on a niche tax regime used by 5% of customers. The vendor says the new model is “much bigger”. What should you expect from upgrading?
o: The niche regime will be fixed, because bigger models know everything
Some improvement is possible, but niche facts thin in public text stay weak; supply them through context or retrieval and measure
No change, because model size has no effect on knowledge
Worse results, because larger models hallucinate more
quiz.w: Pretraining learns in proportion to exposure. Long-tail knowledge improves slowly with scale, so the reliable fix is to put the source material in front of the model and check with an eval.

quiz.q: After a model upgrade, users complain the assistant now agrees with incorrect statements in their questions. Which stage of training most likely shifted?
o: Pretraining data mix
Tokenizer
Preference tuning in post-training
The knowledge cutoff
quiz.w: Sycophancy comes mainly from preference tuning, which rewards agreeable answers. It can change between versions, which is why false-premise cases belong in your regression eval.

quiz.q: A coding agent reports “all tests pass” on a bug fix, and review shows it edited the test to remove the failing assertion. What is the best description?
o: A hallucination caused by the knowledge cutoff
Reward hacking, a known risk of training against verifiable rewards
A tokenization error in the test file
Expected behaviour that needs no action
quiz.w: Models trained with RL on test outcomes can learn to satisfy the checker instead of the task. Review diffs and tests together, and restrict which files the agent may change.

quiz.q: Moving a feature from low to high reasoning effort raises your eval pass rate from 81% to 84% and median latency from 3 to 19 seconds. The feature is an inline suggestion while users type. What should you do?
o: Keep low effort for the inline path, and consider routing only hard cases to high effort or the background
Ship high effort, since accuracy always wins
Turn thinking off entirely to save cost
Increase the max token limit
quiz.w: Test-time compute is a trade. Three points rarely justify a sixfold latency hit on an interactive surface. Route by difficulty and let the eval set the threshold.

quiz.q: Your eval scores a wrong answer and “I don’t know” both as zero. You compare two models with the same accuracy. What risk does this scoring create?
o: None, since accuracy is identical
It overweights latency
It penalises the model for citing sources
It can’t tell a model that abstains when unsure from one that fabricates, and tends to favour guessing
quiz.w: This is the evaluation incentive OpenAI’s hallucination paper identifies. Score abstentions above wrong answers so you select for calibrated behaviour.

quiz.q: You are launching a chat feature in India and Thailand with the same per-message cost budget as in the US. What should you check first?
o: Whether the model’s knowledge cutoff is recent enough
Tokens per message in each language, since non-Latin scripts often use several times more tokens for the same content
Whether temperature should be lowered for those markets
Whether the tokenizer supports emoji
quiz.w: The language premium raises cost, latency and context use. Measure tokens per locale before setting prices and budgets.

deliverable.title: How our model fails: a one-page memo for one product surface
deliverable.html:
Write this from your lab results for the engineers, designers and support leads who work on the surface. Keep it to one page, and refresh it whenever the model changes.

  1. Surface and setup. The feature, the model and version, effort setting, tools and the date of the probe.
  2. Top three failure patterns. For each, one real example (input and output), how often it happened in the probe, and its cause from this chapter: long-tail recall, sycophancy, reward hacking, tokenization, cutoff or context conflict.
  3. Structural versus fixable. Which failures you removed with a cheap change, and which remain because of how the model is built. State plainly that the structural ones need design, not more prompting.
  4. Mitigations in place and proposed. Grounding, citations, abstention, date injection, calculator or code tools, verification steps. Owner and target date for each proposal.
  5. User-facing implications. Where the UI must show sources, uncertainty or a review step, with a link to Chapter 9 patterns.
  6. Regression cases. The prompts from the probe that you are adding to the eval set so these failures are caught on every model or prompt change (Chapter 5).

End with one sentence a support agent can repeat to a customer about what the feature can and can’t be trusted to do.
